words.intro: Rothenburg ob der Tauber is the medieval town everyone imagines. The wall is whole, the night watchman walks at eight, and legend says a mayor once saved it by drinking.

grammar[0].fact: Rothenburg is so well-kept that it was the model for the village in *Pinocchio*, and it’s a regular film set. The Christmas shop is open all year round.

grammar[1].blocks[2].text: *ich ging, er ging* — nothing added. The plural adds -en: *wir gingen, sie gingen*.

grammar[1].fact: Spoken German barely uses this tense, except for *war, hatte* and the helpers. It is what you read in novels, newspapers and fairy tales. A German who tells a friend *Ich ging gestern ins Kino* sounds as if reading aloud.

document.intro: A real bronze plaque on a wall in Dresden. Plaques are where the written past lives. This one is about the composer Richard Wagner, and *Kriegsverlust* means the house was lost in the war.
document.fact: Wagner had to flee Dresden in 1849, after taking part in an uprising, and he stayed away from Germany for many years. Almost every German town has a plaque saying someone famous once slept there. Wagner, who moved often and left debts, has plenty.

reading.intro: Maya takes the night watchman’s tour in Rothenburg. He wears a black cloak, carries a lantern, and tells the town’s most famous story, the *Meistertrunk*. A group from Ohio is delighted. Then a small child at the front asks a question.
reading.fact: The *Meistertrunk* is a legend, first told long after the Thirty Years’ War. The town plays it on stage every Whitsun anyway, and the clock on the square re-enacts it several times a day. Rothenburg survived the Second World War, partly because an American official knew how beautiful it was.
